1.pericope_label: Hear, O Israel: a mightier enemy and a God who goes before

schools.summary: Gill supposes a pause after the preceding discourse, and glosses the Anakim as a people of large bulk and stature beside whom the spies had seemed grasshoppers. Calvin reads the whole passage as a eulogy on God's gratuitous liberality: that Israel should inherit Canaan by no merit but by signal bounty, flowing wholly from the covenant and their free adoption, ought to have ravished them to the worship of a God they owed so much. To leave them nothing to arrogate, Moses magnifies the difficulty — numbers, valour, impregnable cities, the children of Anak — and then cites the people themselves as witnesses, since the spies' report had so terrified them that they wished to turn back. Calvin notes that the giants were known only to a few, but that Moses transfers the case of those few to them all, terror having spread through the whole camp; and he draws the general lesson that such is the ingratitude of mankind that men obscure God's bounties as far as they can, and never yield except when driven to conviction.

Henry finds the striking thing in the opening to be that Moses reports almost exactly what the evil spies had reported, the difference lying wholly in the intention: theirs was to drive the people from God and discourage their hope, this to drive them to God and engage it. He notes that Moses denies their righteousness three times over — not for thy righteousness, not for the uprightness of thy heart, neither for good conversation nor good disposition — because it is hard to bring people off a conceit of their merit and yet necessary that it be done. The two real reasons he draws from God's honour rather than Israel's deserts, and states the asymmetry as sharply as it can be put: all whom God rejects are rejected for their own wickedness, but none whom he accepts are accepted for their own righteousness.

Clarke fixes the moment most exactly of anyone: this day means this time, the people having come near the verge of the land thirty-eight years before and been refused the crossing for their rebellions. He dates the speech to the eleventh month of the fortieth year and the crossing to the month following, and notes that Moses died between. Wesley takes it for a new address on the next sabbath, and explains why the enemy's strength is stressed — so that they should not trust their own strength, and when the work was done should ascribe the glory to God.

Keil identifies the enemy Moses is really fighting, and it is not Canaanite. Besides the vulgar pride that forgets God and credits success to its own exertion, there is a subtler kind which acknowledges God's blessings but, instead of receiving them gratefully as unmerited gifts, sees in them only proofs of its own righteousness. Ellicott glosses the phrase fenced up to heaven by the tower whose top was in the heavens, and wonders whether Paul had it in mind writing of wrestling against wickedness in heavenly places.

debates.question: Why does Moses stress the enemy's strength at all?

positions.position: to drive the people to God and engage their hope in him — the evil spies used the same facts to drive them away
so that they should not trust their own strength and should ascribe the glory to God afterwards

outliers.note: names the refined pride that acknowledges the blessing and still reads it as a proof of desert — the real target of the whole chapter

themes: the same report as the spies, to the opposite purpose
the subtler pride that credits God and still claims merit

2.pericope_label: Not for thy righteousness: a stiffnecked people

schools.summary: Gill glosses the Anakim briefly and repeats the denial of merit. Calvin's exposition of speak not in thine heart is the most careful thing here: to speak in the heart is to reflect, so Moses reproves not the boasting of the lips but the hidden arrogance by which men take to themselves the praise due to God. He then draws a distinction easy to miss — Moses assumes they will grant the victory was God's, but is not content with that limited gratitude unless they also own that they deserved nothing, since God is not less defrauded when men set their righteousness against his liberality than when they boast of their own industry. Calvin also admits a weakness in the argument as stated: that the nations were driven out for wickedness is not on its face conclusive, since God might take from reprobates only to give to worthier men, so he reads the clause as an indirect admonition to compare themselves with those nations. He takes the stiffnecked metaphor from oxen, useless until taught to bend the neck, and adds the decisive chronology — the covenant was made with Abraham almost four centuries before these men were born.

Clarke pushes the reasoning furthest. These peoples were cast out not by a sovereign act but for their wickedness; Israel possessed the land not by desert but because they were less wicked, and because God chose to begin the work of salvation among men there. The Canaanites were cut off and Israel grafted in — and Israel, for their wickedness, cut off afterwards and the Gentiles grafted in, so let these not be high-minded but fear. Yet the land was originally the Canaanites' own, he adds, and the new possessors had no legal right. Wesley reaches the same end in a sentence: neither upright heart nor holy life, the two things God most regards, so all merit is excluded — they who did not deserve an earthly Canaan could not merit glory.

Ellicott hears a structure built on one repeated word: three times the formula occurs — the children of Anak thou knowest, thou knowest the Lord thy God, and thou knowest thyself. The pronouns are emphatic throughout, including in not for thy righteousness dost thou go, where the force is that there is no reason why thou of all people shouldst be so honoured. He takes the stiffnecked metaphor from a camel that hardens its neck and will not bend for the driver. Keil ties the halves of the sentence together grammatically: when Jehovah thrusts these nations out, Israel is not to say within itself that it is for their righteousness, the following clause being adversative.

debates.question: What animal lies behind the stiffnecked metaphor?

positions.position: the ox, useless until taught to bend its neck — so the people not merely refused submission but shook off the yoke
a camel or other beast of burden that hardens its neck and will not bend for the driver

outliers.note: concedes that the reason given is not conclusive on its face, since God might have taken from reprobates only to give to worthier men, and supplies the missing step himself

themes: granting God the victory while still claiming the merit

7.pericope_label: Remember and forget not: the provocation at Horeb

schools.summary: Gill notes with Aben Ezra that the provoking did not begin after Horeb — they murmured for water at Marah when three days in the wilderness, for bread in the wilderness of Sin, and again at Rephidim, all before Sinai. On the tables he dwells on how wholly they were God's work: the letters of his devising, the writing his, the engraving his own doing, which stamped divine authority on the law and denoted its duration. Calvin explains why the story is retold, and in almost the words Moses used in Exodus: to reprove ingratitude, dwelling on the revolt in which their most detestable impiety betrayed itself, and urging them to reflect often on their sins, since constant recollection not only humbles but teaches men at length to lay aside their depraved nature. On the harder question he will not speculate — if it is asked how Moses prevailed on God to change his intention, curiosity must be repressed, since God did not act otherwise than he had determined and Moses goes no deeper than the sentence revealed to him.

Henry makes the purpose plain: lest they think God brought them to Canaan for their righteousness, Moses shows it a miracle of mercy they were not destroyed long since. Their fathers' provocations are charged on this generation, since had God dealt with the fathers by desert these men had never existed, much less entered Canaan. We are apt to forget our provocations, he adds, especially once the smart of the rod is over, and need reminding lest we entertain any conceit of our own righteousness — which is Paul's argument from the guilt of all mankind: if our works condemn us, they will not justify us.

Wesley piles up the aggravations of the calf: their deliverance from Egypt was fresh in memory, God had newly manifested himself in a manner stupendous and dreadful, had just taken them into covenant, and was then conferring further mercies. On the tables he draws the lesson that the finger of God signifies not only that greater reverence was due the law, but that it is God's work alone to write it on the tables of men's hearts.

Ellicott finds the Hebrew blunter than the English — remember, forget not, how thou hast stirred the indignation of Jehovah — and presses the word rendered rebellious, which is not simply rebels, as Moses called them at Meribah, but provoking rebels, who rouse the opposition of him against whom they rebel. He compresses the aggravation to a line: in the very sight of the mountain of the Law, the Law was flagrantly violated. He also notes that Moses neither eating bread nor drinking water during the first forty days is nowhere related in Exodus, where he goes up with his minister Joshua — it might be supposed, but it is not recorded. Keil marks the grammar, the connecting particle bringing the sin into prominence as specially heinous for its circumstances: Moses was on the mountain forty days occupied with the holiest things, at a time when Israel should have been meditating on words they had just heard.

debates.question: How could Moses prevail on God to change his intention?

positions.position: the question must not be pressed — God did not act otherwise than he had determined, and Moses goes no deeper than the sentence revealed to him

outliers.note: notices a small silence in Exodus: the fasting through the first forty days is nowhere recorded there, though it might be supposed

themes: provocations before Horeb as well as after
why the golden calf was so heinous
whether God can be said to change his intention

11.pericope_label: Let me alone: the broken tables and the forty days

schools.summary: Gill points the irony that the omniscient God knew what was doing in the camp though Moses did not, and reads Let me alone as a command not to say one word on their behalf. Calvin is the chronologist of the passage. The order of the narrative is confused, he says, since this fast did not precede the second ascent — else Moses had fasted three times, which other passages show he did not. He insists too on what the fast was not: no sign of mourning, as when Joel calls the people to sackcloth, since abstinence was no more grievous to Moses than to angels, but a sign that so great a sin could not be expiated unless he again renounced the life of men and was taken up to God. On the tables he denies that anger broke them — Moses accuses himself of no transgression, and discharges rather the office of a herald, as the Roman fecial cast a bloody spear into another's territory to declare war, denouncing by solemn rite that God's covenant was broken. On Aaron he sees how vain are the pretexts by which men hide their faults, Aaron pleading compulsion where the greatness of the threatened punishment proves how gross the sin was.

Clarke glosses the charge — they had debased themselves by making and worshipping an Egyptian idol. Wesley is briefest on Let me alone: stop me not by thy intercession. On the tables he agrees the breaking was no unbridled passion but zeal for God's honour and by his Spirit's direction.

Ellicott notes the words summarised here stand at length in Exodus, where Moses's intercession is also recorded, and on ye had turned aside quickly writes that nothing in human experience is so sad as the rapidity with which good resolutions and impressions fade from the natural heart of man. He argues the breaking of the tables was deliberate: Moses did not drop them in passion before reaching the camp, but broke the material covenant before a people who had broken the covenant itself — and remembering what came in later times of touching not the tables but the chest that held them, he thinks it may even have been necessary for Israel's safety, noting that the temporary tabernacle was pitched outside the camp at the same time and seemingly for the same reason. He adds that Joshua was with Moses the first forty days but not the second, and that the words rendered I was afraid are in Greek identical with the I exceedingly fear of Hebrews.

debates.question: Was the breaking of the tables an act of passion?

positions.position: no — deliberate, done before the people’s eyes, and perhaps necessary for Israel’s safety
no — Moses acted as a herald declaring the covenant void by solemn rite, and accuses himself of no transgression
no — zeal for God’s honour and the direction of his Spirit, not unbridled passion

outliers.note: reads the calf as a case study in how fast good impressions fade from the natural heart, which he calls the saddest thing in human experience

themes: whether Moses broke the tables in anger

21.pericope_label: The calf in the brook, the roll of provocations, and the prayer

schools.summary: Gill takes your sin as the object of the sin, which lay in making and worshipping the calf, and worries at the disorder of the place-names without resolving it: Massah came before Sinai and Taberah after, and though Aben Ezra reports some who identify the two, Gill objects that Taberah cannot be the Massah in Rephidim, which lay on the other side of the mount. He would rather identify Taberah with Kibroth-hattaavah, since no removal between them is recorded and only the latter appears in the itinerary. On the fasts he reports Jarchi's view that this is the fast already mentioned, repeated for the order of the prayer, notes that at the first is not in the text, and inclines with the Jewish writers and Lightfoot to a third forty days. Calvin reads the roll of places morally — Moses convicts them of ingratitude and obstinacy, the names standing as memorials of their sins — and holds the narrative simply blended, the prayer having been offered before the second fast though folded into it, since a man may still tremble after obtaining the safety he asked for.

Wesley notes the dust was cast into the brook that no monument of it might be left. Clarke dwells on the appeal to the patriarchs, as if Moses said these are their descendants and the covenant was made on their behalf; from which he draws that God bestows many blessings on worthless persons for the sake of pious ancestors, or of the religious people they are joined to, so that union with the church is no common blessing.

Ellicott sees the identifying of sin with the material object as of a piece with the law in Leviticus, where sin and sin-offering are denoted by one word, and then makes the observation that lifts the verse: the stream from the rock in Horeb not only gave Israel drink but bore their sin away on its waters — and that Rock was Christ. He turns the disorder of the place-names into design, Taberah being the first place named after Sinai and Massah the last before it, so that Sinai is made the centre of provocation; and on the prayer he notices the pronouns, God having said to Moses thy people, which thou broughtest out, have corrupted themselves, and Moses answering, why doth thy wrath wax hot against thy people, which thou hast brought forth. Keil finds design in the order too, but a different one: the list is not chronological but advances by degrees from the slighter to the graver forms of guilt, to sharpen the people's consciences.

debates.question: Why are Taberah, Massah and Kibroth-hattaavah listed out of chronological order?

positions.position: the list ascends from the slighter to the graver forms of guilt, to sharpen the conscience
the arrangement makes Sinai the centre — Taberah the first place after it, Massah the last before it
the disorder is real and not fully resolvable; Taberah is probably Kibroth-hattaavah

debates.question: Was there a third forty-day fast?

positions.position: yes — with the Jewish writers and Lightfoot
no — the narrative is blended, and prayers offered earlier are folded into the second fast

outliers.note: reads the brook that carried off the calf's dust as the stream from the smitten rock, and so as Christ bearing away the sin it dissolved

themes: the calf ground to dust and carried off by the brook
